description: A composite two-part figure. The dominant panel is an engineering stress–strain plot: x-axis "Engineering plastic strain (%)" 0–50 (ticks every 5), y-axis "Engineering stress (MPa)" 0–1200. Several near-parallel black curves run as a flat plateau just above the 1000 MPa gridline and fracture between roughly the 40% and 45% strain gridlines; a red curve (arrow-labelled) lies marginally below them and fractures first, near the 40% gridline. Arrows and bold labels identify the groups: black arrow "Without hydrogen charging", red arrow "With hydrogen charging". No numeric strength or strain values are printed on any curve. The inset is a thermal desorption analysis (TDA) spectrum: x-axis "temperature, °C" (0, 300, 600, 900) and y-axis "hydrogen desorption rate (wt ppm/s)" with ticks 0.0, 5.0×10⁻⁵, 1.0×10⁻⁴, 1.5×10⁻⁴, 2.0×10⁻⁴; annotation "heating rate 26K/min"; legend "experiment" (solid line), "peak fit" (dashed line), "cumulative fit" (open circles). The experimental trace shows a small low-temperature feature near 200–300 °C and two dominant overlapping peaks, the lower one near 500 °C and the taller near 650 °C, each reproduced by a dashed peak-fit component. The group argues that hydrogen charging produces only a small loss of strength but a clearer loss of ductility, while desorption occurs from several distinct trapping states; no values are printed on either panel.

observations.observation: The main panel is an engineering stress–strain plot with x-axis 'Engineering plastic strain (%)' spanning 0–50 and y-axis 'Engineering stress (MPa)' spanning 0–1200.

All stress–strain curves lie on a long plateau immediately above the 1000 MPa gridline and terminate between roughly 40% and 45% engineering plastic strain; no numeric fracture stress or strain is printed.
A black arrow and label 'Without hydrogen charging' identify the upper curve group, which reaches the highest plateau and the latest fracture.
A red arrow and label 'With hydrogen charging' identify the curve lying slightly below the black group, which fractures at a lower strain (close to the 40% gridline).
The inset TDA plot has axes 'temperature, °C' (ticks 0, 300, 600, 900) and 'hydrogen desorption rate (wt ppm/s)' (ticks 0.0 to 2.0×10⁻⁴).
The inset carries the annotation 'heating rate 26K/min' and a legend with 'experiment' (solid line), 'peak fit' (dashed line) and 'cumulative fit' (open circles).

The experimental desorption trace shows two dominant overlapping peaks, the lower near 500 °C and the taller near 650 °C, plus a weak low-temperature feature near 200–300 °C; the peak fits resolve these as separate dashed components.
The caption states that hydrogen was introduced by precharging for 40 min and by permanent in situ hydrogen charging imposed also during the ongoing tests.
The caption states that the inset shows results obtained from thermal desorption analysis taken at a heating rate of 26 K/min.
The caption does not state which specimen (charged or uncharged) the TDA inset corresponds to, and the panel itself carries no such label.

The citing text reports that Koyama et al. (ref 59) observed by thermal desorption analysis that κ-carbides (written 'j-carbides') can act as hydrogen trap sites, with an estimated activation energy of 76–80 kJ/mol from a Redlich–Kister analysis.
The caption notes the figure is a colour figure online, consistent with the black/red colour coding used to distinguish charging conditions in the stress–strain panel.

subfigures.description: Engineering stress–strain curves, stress (MPa, 0–1200) vs plastic strain (%, 0–50). A group of black curves plateauing just above 1000 MPa and fracturing at ~40–45% strain is arrow-labelled 'Without hydrogen charging'; a red curve slightly below them, fracturing near 40% strain, is arrow-labelled 'With hydrogen charging'. Curve counts are not resolvable.

Thermal desorption analysis spectrum, hydrogen desorption rate (wt ppm/s, 0 to 2.0×10⁻⁴) vs temperature (°C, 0–900), annotated 'heating rate 26K/min'. Legend: solid = experiment, dashed = peak fit, open circles = cumulative fit. Two dominant overlapping peaks near 500 °C and 650 °C plus a weak low-temperature shoulder near 200–300 °C.
